title: History and Life of Camel Caravans
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: A camel train is a group of camels carrying passengers and goods across deserts. For centuries, camels could walk through harsh places where other travel was very hard. They were used for trade and communication in parts of Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.
pages.caption: A contemporary camel caravan for salt transportation in Lake Karum in Afar Region, Ethiopia

evidence.fileTitle: File:Salt transport by a camel train on Lake Assale (Karum) in Ethiopia.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A contemporary camel caravan for salt transportation in Lake Karum in Afar Region, Ethiopia

pages.text: The greatest use of camel trains happens in North and West Africa. Groups like the Tuareg and Toubou travel around the Sahara Desert and the Sahel. These caravans go as far south as Nigeria and Cameroon, and to Kenya in the east of the continent.
pages.caption: Ancient Roman mosaic depicting a merchant leading a camel train. Bosra, Syria

evidence.articleCaption: Ancient Roman mosaic depicting a merchant leading a camel train. Bosra, Syria

pages.text: Camel trains were also very important in Asia, including the Silk Road. In China, camel caravans connected eastern regions with Mongolia and Xinjiang. Owen Lattimore travelled with a camel caravan in China in 1926 to study the trade routes.
pages.caption: Camel train transporting a house, Kalgoorlie, Western Australia, ca. 1928

evidence.articleCaption: Camel train transporting a house, Kalgoorlie, Western Australia, ca. 1928

pages.text: In Australia, a famous camel train service connected a railhead in South Australia to Alice Springs. The service ended in 1929 when a new railway line was built. The route was originally made by Afghan cameleers.
pages.caption: Camel convoy in the Jordan Rift Valley, West Bank, May 2010

evidence.articleCaption: Camel convoy in the Jordan Rift Valley, West Bank, May 2010

pages.text: The United States Army tried using camels in Texas in 1856. The experiment failed because the animals were stubborn and frightened horses. Many camels were sold or escaped into the desert, where people saw them for many years.

B1-B2.headline: History and Life of Camel Caravans

pages.text: A camel train, also known as a caravan, is a series of camels that carry passengers and goods on regular routes. Because camels could withstand harsh desert conditions, they were ideal for communication and trade in North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula for centuries.
pages.caption: A contemporary camel caravan for salt transportation in Lake Karum in Afar Region, Ethiopia

evidence.fileTitle: File:Salt transport by a camel train on Lake Assale (Karum) in Ethiopia.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A contemporary camel caravan for salt transportation in Lake Karum in Afar Region, Ethiopia

pages.text: By far, the greatest use of camel trains occurs between North and West Africa. Groups such as the Tuareg, Shuwa, and Hassaniyya conduct trade in and around the Sahara Desert and Sahel, traveling as far south as Nigeria and Cameroon in the west, and northern Kenya in the east. Since the early twentieth century, they have been largely replaced by motorized vehicles or air traffic.
pages.caption: Ancient Roman mosaic depicting a merchant leading a camel train. Bosra, Syria

evidence.articleCaption: Ancient Roman mosaic depicting a merchant leading a camel train. Bosra, Syria

pages.text: Camel trains were also used extensively in trans-Asian trade, including the Silk Road. As late as the early twentieth century, caravans connected eastern China with Mongolian centers and Xinjiang. Owen Lattimore documented these northern routes in 1926.
pages.caption: Camel train transporting a house, Kalgoorlie, Western Australia, ca. 1928

evidence.articleCaption: Camel train transporting a house, Kalgoorlie, Western Australia, ca. 1928

pages.text: In the United States, the Army attempted a camel transport experiment in Texas. On April 29, 1856, thirty-three camels and five drivers arrived at Indianola. The project ultimately failed because the animals were aggressive and frightened horses. Some camels were sold, while others escaped to live as feral animals.
pages.caption: Camel convoy in the Jordan Rift Valley, West Bank, May 2010

evidence.articleCaption: Camel convoy in the Jordan Rift Valley, West Bank, May 2010

pages.text: Caravans were organized into files of camels led by camel-pullers who were experts in animal health and care. The journey required careful logistical planning, including food, fodder, and shelter, as trips through harsh regions could take many months.

C1-C2.headline: The Organization and Routes of Camel Trains

pages.text: A camel train or caravan functions as a systematic series of camels transporting goods and passengers across challenging terrains. Historically valued for their resilience in harsh environments, camel trains facilitated vital communication and trade networks primarily across North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula before being largely supplanted by motorized transport.
pages.caption: A contemporary camel caravan for salt transportation in Lake Karum in Afar Region, Ethiopia

evidence.fileTitle: File:Salt transport by a camel train on Lake Assale (Karum) in Ethiopia.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A contemporary camel caravan for salt transportation in Lake Karum in Afar Region, Ethiopia

pages.text: Extensive contemporary and historical documentation highlights the concentration of camel trains in North and West Africa, operated by groups including the Tuareg, Shuwa, and Toubou. These caravans traverse the Sahara and Sahel, reaching deep into central Nigeria, northern Cameroon, and northern Kenya.
pages.caption: Ancient Roman mosaic depicting a merchant leading a camel train. Bosra, Syria

evidence.articleCaption: Ancient Roman mosaic depicting a merchant leading a camel train. Bosra, Syria

pages.text: Trans-Asian trade routes, most notably the Silk Road, heavily relied on camel caravans. Into the early twentieth century, these networks connected eastern Chinese regions with Mongolian trade hubs and Xinjiang, a dynamic closely observed and recorded by researcher Owen Lattimore during his 1926 expedition.
pages.caption: Camel train transporting a house, Kalgoorlie, Western Australia, ca. 1928

evidence.articleCaption: Camel train transporting a house, Kalgoorlie, Western Australia, ca. 1928

pages.text: Operations in the United States were largely limited to a mid-nineteenth-century United States Army experiment initiated in Texas. Due to behavioral challenges such as stubbornness and aggressiveness toward horses, the initiative dissolved, leading to sales and escapes that established feral camel populations in the region.
pages.caption: Camel convoy in the Jordan Rift Valley, West Bank, May 2010

evidence.articleCaption: Camel convoy in the Jordan Rift Valley, West Bank, May 2010

pages.text: Caravan structures were complex, often managed by a definitive captain alongside experienced camel-pullers who maintained animal health and navigation. Journeys required substantial provisions, including specific camel fodder and careful management of loads, speeds, and rest periods across vast desert expanses.

title: Understanding Mass Spectrometry
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Mass spectrometry is a scientific tool. It measures the mass and charge of tiny particles in a sample. Scientists use it to learn what a sample is made of. The results appear as a chart called a mass spectrum.
pages.caption: Discovery of neon isotopes

evidence.articleCaption: Discovery of neon isotopes

pages.text: First, a sample is turned into ions. This means the particles get an electric charge or break into charged pieces. Next, these ions move through electric or magnetic fields. Particles with different mass and charge move in different ways.
pages.caption: Replica of F.W. Aston's third mass spectrometer

evidence.articleCaption: Replica of F.W. Aston's third mass spectrometer

pages.text: A detector finds the charged particles at the end of the process. The system displays the final data as a spectrum chart. Researchers look at the known masses and patterns to identify the atoms and molecules.
pages.caption: Surface ionization source at the Argonne National Laboratory linear accelerator

evidence.articleCaption: Surface ionization source at the Argonne National Laboratory linear accelerator

pages.text: Mass spectrometry includes five main parts. These parts are the sample inlet, the ion source, the mass analyzer, the detector, and a data system. Each part can work independently to provide good flexibility for tests.
pages.caption: Quadrupole mass spectrometer and electrospray ion source used for Fenn's early work

evidence.articleCaption: Quadrupole mass spectrometer and electrospray ion source used for Fenn's early work

pages.text: History shows early work began long ago. In 1886, Eugen Goldstein found canal rays in gas discharges. Later scientists improved these devices to study particles. Today, researchers apply this technique across many different fields.

Mass spectrometry is an analytical technique used to measure the mass-to-charge ratio of ions. The output is a mass spectrum, which plots signal intensity against this ratio. Researchers use these spectra to determine elemental signatures, particle masses, and the chemical structure of molecules in pure samples or complex mixtures.
pages.caption: Discovery of neon isotopes

evidence.articleCaption: Discovery of neon isotopes

pages.text: During a typical procedure, a solid, liquid, or gaseous sample is ionized by methods such as an electron beam. This process creates charged particles or fragments. An electric or magnetic field then separates these ions because particles with identical mass-to-charge ratios undergo the same amount of deflection.
pages.caption: Replica of F.W. Aston's third mass spectrometer

evidence.articleCaption: Replica of F.W. Aston's third mass spectrometer

pages.text: A detector records the separated ions. Scientists then identify the atoms or molecules by matching known masses to the identified values or by analyzing characteristic fragmentation patterns. Early instruments recorded these values on photographic plates or phosphor screens.
pages.caption: Surface ionization source at the Argonne National Laboratory linear accelerator

evidence.articleCaption: Surface ionization source at the Argonne National Laboratory linear accelerator

pages.text: Every mass spectrometer consists of five core components: a sample inlet, an ion source, a mass analyzer, a detector, and a data system. Because these components can vary independently, the instrument offers great flexibility in analytical pipelines.
pages.caption: Quadrupole mass spectrometer and electrospray ion source used for Fenn's early work

evidence.articleCaption: Quadrupole mass spectrometer and electrospray ion source used for Fenn's early work

pages.text: The history of the field dates back to the late nineteenth century. Eugen Goldstein observed canal rays in 1886, and Wilhelm Wien later built a device to separate positive rays using perpendicular fields. J. J. Thomson subsequently improved this design by reducing pressure to create the mass spectrograph.

C1-C2.headline: Principles and Components of Mass Spectrometry

pages.text: Mass spectrometry is an analytical methodology designed to quantify the mass-to-charge ratio of ions, yielding a mass spectrum that charts signal intensity against this ratio. This framework enables researchers to elucidate isotopic signatures, molecular masses, and chemical structures across pure substances and intricate mixtures alike.
pages.caption: Discovery of neon isotopes

evidence.articleCaption: Discovery of neon isotopes

pages.text: The analytical workflow requires ionizing a solid, liquid, or gaseous sample via techniques such as electron bombardment. The resulting ions or molecular fragments are subsequently subjected to electric or magnetic fields, causing ions with equivalent mass-to-charge ratios to experience uniform deflection trajectories.
pages.caption: Replica of F.W. Aston's third mass spectrometer

evidence.articleCaption: Replica of F.W. Aston's third mass spectrometer

pages.text: Detection mechanisms, including electron multipliers, register the deflected ions. Analysts identify constituent particles by correlating empirical mass values with known reference data or by evaluating specific fragmentation patterns. Historically, early instruments utilized photographic plates or phosphor screens to record these spectra.
pages.caption: Surface ionization source at the Argonne National Laboratory linear accelerator

evidence.articleCaption: Surface ionization source at the Argonne National Laboratory linear accelerator

pages.text: Instrumentation is modular, comprising five distinct functional components: a sample inlet, an ion source, a mass analyzer, a detector, and a data system. Each unit operates with relative independence, permitting substantial configuration flexibility within broader analytical pipelines.
pages.caption: Quadrupole mass spectrometer and electrospray ion source used for Fenn's early work

evidence.articleCaption: Quadrupole mass spectrometer and electrospray ion source used for Fenn's early work

pages.text: Historical developments originated with Eugen Goldstein's observation of canal rays in 1886. Wilhelm Wien advanced the field by constructing a device using perpendicular fields to separate positive ions according to their charge-to-mass ratio, a foundation that J. J. Thomson refined into early mass spectrographs.

Mass analyzers utilize diverse static or dynamic electric and magnetic configurations to separate ions. Key performance metrics include mass resolving power, which defines the smallest detectable difference in the mass-to-charge ratio, typically quantified via the full width at half maximum of a given spectral peak.

title: Geography of Rwanda
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Rwanda is a small country in East Africa. It is near the Equator, but its high mountains give it a cool, nice climate. The land has no ocean coast. It shares borders with Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
pages.caption: Enlargeable, detailed map of Rwanda

evidence.articleCaption: Enlargeable, detailed map of Rwanda

pages.text: People call Rwanda the land of a thousand hills. From west to east, the land goes from high mountains to a central plateau and then to eastern lowlands. Mount Karisimbi is the highest peak in the country. The lowest point is the Rusizi River.
pages.caption: Relief of Rwanda

evidence.articleCaption: Relief of Rwanda

pages.text: Rain and rivers shape the land. Most water flows east to the Nile basin through rivers like the Kagera. Some water flows west to the Congo basin. Lake Kivu sits on the western border. Smaller lakes are found across the interior.
pages.caption: Topographic map of Rwanda

evidence.articleCaption: Topographic map of Rwanda

pages.text: The country has rich plant and animal life. Its nature areas include mountain forests, savannas, and wetlands. Akagera National Park protects eastern wildlife. Conservation challenges include wetland loss, poaching, and land erosion from heavy rains.
pages.caption: Rain in Kigali (January 2020)

evidence.fileTitle: File:A man walks through heavy rain under an umbrella in Kigali, Rwanda. Emmanuel Kwizera.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Rain in Kigali (January 2020)

pages.text: Rwanda has a very large population for its size. A recent census recorded over thirteen million residents. Most people live in rural areas, while the capital city, Kigali, holds many urban residents. Life expectancy at birth reached nearly seventy years.

Because it is landlocked, Rwanda relies on trade routes through neighboring countries to reach the sea. The Central Corridor connects the nation to Tanzania and the port of Dar es Salaam, while the Northern Corridor links it to Kenya.

Rwanda is a landlocked nation located in the Eastern African highlands, just south of the Equator. Bounded by Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the country covers a compact territory with no coastline. Its high elevation tempers its equatorial location, creating a mild tropical highland climate across its diverse landscape.
pages.caption: Enlargeable, detailed map of Rwanda

evidence.articleCaption: Enlargeable, detailed map of Rwanda

pages.text: The national topography transitions from west to east across three main divisions. Western Rwanda features the steep Albertine Rift mountains and the Virunga volcanoes, including Mount Karisimbi, the highest point at 4,507 metres. A central plateau of rolling hills follows, earning the nation its famous nickname, while the eastern edge descends into drier savannas and lowlands.
pages.caption: Relief of Rwanda

evidence.articleCaption: Relief of Rwanda

pages.text: A major north-south watershed divides the country into two distinct drainage basins. Approximately eighty percent of Rwanda drains eastward into the Nile basin through systems like the Nyabarongo and Kagera rivers, while twenty percent drains westward toward the Congo basin, primarily through Lake Kivu and the Rusizi River. Numerous lakes dot the interior landscape.
pages.caption: Topographic map of Rwanda

evidence.articleCaption: Topographic map of Rwanda

pages.text: Ecosystems range from mountain forests in the west to wetlands and savannas in the east, supporting notable biodiversity. However, dense human settlement and highland farming put intense pressure on natural resources. Challenges such as soil erosion on steep slopes, deforestation, wetland degradation, and poaching threaten these delicate environments.
pages.caption: Rain in Kigali (January 2020)

evidence.fileTitle: File:A man walks through heavy rain under an umbrella in Kigali, Rwanda. Emmanuel Kwizera.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Rain in Kigali (January 2020)

pages.text: The population is large and fast-growing, with a high density recorded in recent census data. While the vast majority of residents live in rural areas, urban populations concentrate heavily in Kigali, the national capital. Administrative governance is divided into four provinces and the capital city, which are further subdivided into local districts.

Without maritime access, external trade depends heavily on regional transport corridors. The Central Corridor connects Rwanda through Tanzania to the port of Dar es Salaam, while the Northern Corridor links the country via Uganda and Kenya to the port of Mombasa, securing vital economic ties.

Positioned within the Eastern African highlands just south of the Equator, Rwanda occupies a landlocked territory spanning over twenty-six thousand square kilometres. Bordered by four nations without any direct maritime access, the country's physical character is fundamentally shaped by its positioning along the western branch of the East African Rift and its considerable average elevation, which modifies its equatorial climate into a temperate tropical highland regime.
pages.caption: Enlargeable, detailed map of Rwanda

evidence.articleCaption: Enlargeable, detailed map of Rwanda

pages.text: Geomorphologically, the terrain traverses distinct longitudinal zones from west to east. The western border hosts the Albertine Rift mountains and the volcanic Virunga chain, culminating in Mount Karisimbi at 4,507 metres. Moving eastward, the topography yields to a dissected central plateau of rolling hills and steep ridges—inspiring the sobriquet 'Land of a Thousand Hills'—before terminating in the low-lying savannas and wetlands of the Akagera basin.
pages.caption: Relief of Rwanda

evidence.articleCaption: Relief of Rwanda

pages.text: Hydrologically, a prominent north-south watershed along the western highlands bifurcates the national territory. Eighty percent of runoff directs eastward into the Nile watershed via the Nyabarongo-Kagera river systems, whereas twenty percent discharges westward into the Congo basin through Lake Kivu and the Rusizi River. This intricate drainage network includes multiple interior lakes and notable altitudinal extremes down to the Rusizi River valley.
pages.caption: Topographic map of Rwanda

evidence.articleCaption: Topographic map of Rwanda

pages.text: Despite its modest geographic extent, Rwanda sustains diverse ecological zones, encompassing montane forests in the west and savanna habitats in the east. Nevertheless, intensive subsistence agriculture on vulnerable volcanic soils, coupled with dense demographic pressures, drives severe environmental degradation. Principal ecological concerns include soil exhaustion, deforestation, wetland impairment, and widespread poaching.
pages.caption: Rain in Kigali (January 2020)

evidence.fileTitle: File:A man walks through heavy rain under an umbrella in Kigali, Rwanda. Emmanuel Kwizera.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Rain in Kigali (January 2020)

pages.text: Demographic indicators underscore significant societal dynamics, evidenced by a high population density accompanying the 2022 census results. Administrationally structured into four provinces alongside the capital city of Kigali and further partitioned into local districts, the nation remains predominantly rural, with urbanization largely localized within the capital.

Deprived of a coastline, Rwanda's external commerce relies entirely on overland transit routes. Economic integration within the East African Community relies fundamentally on the Central Corridor, linking the country to the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam, and the Northern Corridor, providing access to the Kenyan port of Mombasa through Uganda.

pages.text: The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations is a foundation. It takes money from many groups. It uses this money to pay for research to make new vaccines against dangerous and emerging infectious diseases.
pages.caption: Launch of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, CEPI in 2017 at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland

evidence.articleCaption: Launch of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, CEPI in 2017 at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland

pages.text: CEPI was conceived in 2015 and launched in 2017 at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. It was co-founded with funding from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the Wellcome Trust, and the governments of India and Norway.
pages.caption: Jeremy Farrar, co-author of the concept of CEPI, and board member

evidence.articleCaption: Jeremy Farrar, co-author of the concept of CEPI, and board member

pages.text: The group focuses on big diseases and unknown threats called Disease X. Its goal is to help the world make a new vaccine very fast when a new pandemic threat happens.
pages.caption: The struggle to get access to vaccine in the 2013–2016 Ebola epidemic was one of the factors motivating the creation of the CEPI.

evidence.articleCaption: The struggle to get access to vaccine in the 2013–2016 Ebola epidemic was one of the factors motivating the creation of the CEPI.

pages.text: At its start, founders promised four hundred sixty million dollars. Later, other governments and groups gave more money. This made it a very large vaccine development project for potential epidemics.
pages.caption: Richard J. Hatchett, CEO of CEPI from 2017

evidence.articleCaption: Richard J. Hatchett, CEO of CEPI from 2017

pages.text: In 2020, people saw the group as very important in the work to develop vaccines for coronavirus disease. Officials and staff run the organisation from its office in Oslo, Norway.

The founding goal of CEPI was equitable access during pandemics, aiming to provide vaccines to developing nations at affordable prices. Later, some rules changed because companies felt the old rules did not fit business realities. CEPI stated its vaccines would still be affordable and available.

The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, known as CEPI, is a foundation that accepts donations from public, private, and philanthropic organizations. It uses these funds to finance independent research projects aimed at developing vaccines against emerging infectious diseases.

pages.text: CEPI focuses on priority diseases identified by the World Health Organization. These include MERS, SARS-CoV-2, Nipah virus, Lassa fever, Rift Valley fever, Chikungunya, and the hypothetical unknown pathogen known as Disease X. In 2022, CEPI adopted a vision enabling the world to respond to a pandemic threat with a new vaccine within one hundred days.

pages.text: The idea for CEPI was outlined in a 2015 medical journal paper. Founders and industry leaders noted that the vaccine market faces severe capacity shortages during health emergencies because epidemics do not occur often enough to maintain spare commercial production lines.

pages.text: At its launch, funders pledged four hundred sixty million dollars, aiming for a one billion dollar target for its first five years. Nature described it as by far the largest vaccine development initiative ever created against potential epidemic threats.

CEPI has experienced policy evolution. Its original contracts included strict rules on intellectual property and pricing transparency, but pharmaceutical companies objected, leading to policy adjustments in late 2018 that removed certain provisions while retaining step-in rights.

The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations operates as a foundation financing independent research initiatives to formulate vaccines against emerging infectious diseases. It relies on financial contributions originating from public, private, philanthropic, and civil society sectors.

pages.text: Initial five-year pledges reached four hundred sixty million dollars, subsequently scaling upward through additional sovereign and philanthropic donations.
